title: Creation, every moment (ST I.104)
hook: God doesn't just start the world; he holds it in being now

segments.voice: Yesterday, he who is: Thomas says the fittest name for God is the one given at the burning bush. Your line was being itself. Where did you stop long enough to say, God is? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

A lamp is on in a room at night. Switch it off and the room goes dark at once. The light doesn't hang around for a minute out of habit. A room is lit only while something is shining into it. Now set that next to the word creation. It's easy to hear creation as an event far back: a first morning, God starting things up and then, maybe, stepping back to watch them run. Thomas Aquinas thought that picture leaves out the part that matters most to him. Today's word is creation, and Thomas wants it in the present tense.
screen: `A ROOM LIT ONLY WHILE LIGHT SHINES.` → `CREATION: A FIRST MORNING?` → `THOMAS: THE PRESENT TENSE.`

segments.voice: In the Summa, Thomas asks whether creatures need God to keep them in being. His answer is yes: every creature, every moment. His image is the sun and the air. The air is bright while the sun shines on it. The brightness isn't something the air owns; take the sun away and the air is dark. So it is, he says, between God and everything that exists. A house keeps standing after the builder goes home, because the builder only arranged bricks that were already there. God doesn't arrange what was already there. He gives things their being, and being isn't something a creature can hold up by itself. Thomas cites Augustine here: if the Creator's power ever stopped, all things would stop with it. Remember from the first way: Thomas says reason alone can't prove the world had a beginning in time. He holds that it did, but by faith. So for Thomas, creation is first of all not a date. It's dependence: being held. And keeping things in being, he says, isn't a second act God adds later. It's the same act that gives being, simply continuing. Scripture says something close. The Letter to the Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims, speaks of Christ "upholding all things by the word of his power." And Paul tells the Athenians: "For in him we live, and move, and are." Put this beside yesterday. If God is being itself, then everything else has its being from him, not once, but now. The chair under you. Your hands. The person who annoyed you this morning. Not wound up and left running. Held. This week walked through the five ways, God's simplicity, how we talk about God, and the name he who is. Today all of that comes down to the floor you're sitting on.
screen: `THE SUN AND THE BRIGHT AIR.` · `A BUILDER LEAVES. GOD DOESN'T.` · `NOT A DATE, BUT DEPENDENCE.` · `THE SAME ACT, CONTINUING.` · then, large: `FOR IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE, AND ARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice you're held in being. Settle, and breathe. Feel the weight of your body on the chair or the floor. Something is holding you up, and you aren't the one doing it. Let that be the doorway. Then go one layer deeper. Not just your weight, but your being here at all. Your breath arrives without being asked. Your heart keeps its own time. Stay with that for a while, without trying to explain it. If you pray, you can say the line from Acts slowly: in him we live, and move, and are. If you don't, simply rest in the fact that this moment was handed to you. The bell holds the time.
Creation. For Thomas, not only a beginning long ago, but God giving everything its being, right now, the way the sun keeps the air bright. Today's word.

Your line: held now. Today, once, when your hand rests on something solid, a cup, a railing, another hand, remember that it's held in being this very moment. That's the week. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics profess God as creator of heaven and earth in the Creed at Mass, and teachers in the tradition of Thomas often explain creation as God's ongoing gift of being, not only a first event.

goes home; the house still stands

myth: for Thomas, creation only means the world's first moment
for Thomas, creation is first of all dependence: God gives things their being now, not only once.
for Thomas, keeping things in being is the same act that gives them being, continuing
it isn't a second act God adds later; the gift of being simply goes on.
in Thomas's picture, God is like a builder who can go home
the house outlasts the builder. creatures don't outlast God's gift of being: take the sun away and the air goes dark.

fork.setup: you're Thomas. a student says: God made the world long ago, and now it runs on its own, like a house after the builder leaves. what do you answer?
options: say the world needs God to keep it in being, as the air needs the sun to stay bright.
say the world was never created at all.
fork.reveal: Thomas answers that every creature depends on God for its being at every moment. the builder picture fits arranging bricks, not giving being.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: creation, the making of something's being.

trapdoor: what you thought: creation is something that happened at the beginning.
what it means: for Thomas, creatures depend on God for their being at every moment, as bright air depends on the sun.
what a scholar hears: Thomas says God keeps things in being not by a new action but by continuing the very act that gives them being.
recall: toward God, for his own sake

sources.ref: Summa Theologiae I, q. 104, a. 1 (with ad 4)

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: the sun-and-air image and the builder/house contrast (I.104.1); the citation of Augustine that all things would cease if the Creator's power ceased (I.104.1); conservation as a continuation of the act that gives being, not a new action (I.104.1 ad 4); that the world's beginning in time is held by faith and not demonstrable (I.46.2).
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Hebrews 1:3 ('upholding all things by the word of his power'); Acts 17:28 ('For in him we live, and move, and are').
Week boundary: this day closes the week of days 1156–1162 (the five ways, simplicity, naming God, he who is, creation); the carry says 'that's the week'.
The light-switch hook is modern; Thomas's own image (sun and air) is given in the teach.

Editor: hook no longer opens on a light switch (day 1156's carry used one); the beginning-in-time point now recalls day 1156 instead of presenting it as new, and the repeated myth item on it was replaced with one on conservation as the same continuing act (I.104.1 ad 4).
